title: Strat Chat: Interleaving
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This article offers a practitioner-level account of how interleaving — mixing questions from multiple topics or units within a single practice session — strengthens long-term retention by increasing cognitive friction and demanding retrieval from different schemas in long-term memory. The author, a classroom teacher, explains how interleaved practice differs from blocked practice and why the short-term performance dip it produces paradoxically produces stronger learning over time. The article is refreshingly honest about implementation constraints: the author rarely achieves the idealised fortnightly interleaved lesson, typically managing one or two such sessions per month depending on curriculum pressure. Practical detail covers how to use past assessment data to identify areas of highest need, how to structure question slides with more questions than time allows for flexibility, and how to reintroduce scaffolding when content was initially learned poorly. The piece closes with a homework suggestion using the same interleaved logic to extend spaced retrieval practice beyond the classroom.
points: Interleaving mixes practice questions from multiple topics within a single session rather than blocked practice of one topic at a time. The resulting cognitive friction — needing to retrieve from different long-term memory schemas per question — produces more effortful and therefore stronger retrieval connections.

The short-term performance cost of interleaving (students feel and perform worse in the session) is a feature, not a bug: it signals the kind of effortful retrieval that leads to durable long-term retention compared to the false fluency of blocked practice.

Planning interleaved lessons using past assessment data to identify areas of highest need allows the teacher to be strategic rather than random — targeting the content where students most require repeated spaced retrieval.

Building slide decks with more questions than the allotted time allows creates responsive flexibility: the teacher can explore some areas more deeply, skip content students have mastered, and insert reachback into any lesson where unexpected time becomes available.

Where content was originally learned poorly, interleaved practice alone is insufficient — a short element of re-teaching should precede the retrieval practice for that content, since students cannot benefit from spacing and interleaving of content they never properly encoded.
quotes: During interleaved lessons, by mixing up the order of questions from different areas of study, it increases the cognitive friction caused by responding as students need to retrieve information from different schemas in their long term memory, which leads to more effortful retrieval and therefore stronger connections formed for future retrieval.

In planning these interleaved lessons I like to use past assessment data to inform areas of highest need for repeated practice mixed in with some simpler questions to guarantee student success and therefore motivation.

They often end up having far more questions than could ever be answered in the required time of varying challenge. This allows me to be responsive and explore some areas more in future or use parts of the deck when there is extra time in lessons throughout the year to ensure there is no wasted learning time.

Sometimes on content which original performance was poor I will include an element of re-teaching before checking for understanding as students are unlikely to see any benefit from the interleaving of that content if they do not know it in the first place.

This would also begin in a highly scaffolded form the first times content reappears before slowly reducing the scaffolding throughout the years interleaved lessons as the students hopefully achieve mastery of all content throughout the unit.
